title: The Leaning Chimney

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, First Saying: A line is only as honest as the hand that holds it.*

On the morning she was supposed to learn whether she had a future, Isla Corrin was lying flat on her stomach on the roof of the Meridian Guild with one eye pressed to a brass sightglass, trying to decide whether the chimney of the Royal Mint was leaning or whether the entire city of Vell was.

It was not yet six. The sun had only just cleared the hills to the east, and the whole capital lay below her in a pearl-coloured haze of coal smoke and bread-oven steam, ten thousand chimneys exhaling at once like a congregation of sleepy giants. The Guild bells were working their way through the hour in the stately, slightly smug manner of bells that had never once been wrong. Isla did not look up at them. She was sixteen, her hair was coming out of its knot despite the two crossed brass pencils that were meant to hold it, there was ink to the second knuckle of every finger on her right hand, and the stone beneath her ribs had been cold enough overnight to leave a pattern on her sleeve.

She turned the fine-adjustment screw a quarter of a degree and read the angle. She wrote it down. She turned the screw back, looked again, and wrote down a second number, which was not quite the same as the first, and which she found quietly insulting.

Three readings, four seconds of arc apart. In a city of ten thousand chimneys, who would care? Isla would. It was, her father liked to say, her particular affliction: she could not leave a crooked thing crooked, and she could not leave a straight thing alone until she had proved it.
pages.image: Dawn on the flat grey-slate roof of a grand stone guild hall above a smoky hill-city of countless chimneys; Isla, a sixteen-year-old girl with light-brown skin and long dark-auburn hair twisted in a high knot held by two crossed brass pencils, in a mustard-yellow canvas surveyor's coat, dark-green trousers and brown buckled boots, lies flat on her stomach with one eye at a brass sightglass on a tripod, a small brass compass on a cord at her neck, the tall chimney of a grey mint in the golden haze below.

pages.text:
Everyone at the Meridian Guild understood what a map was, and nearly everyone at the Meridian Guild understood it wrongly. To the public, a map was a handy picture of the country, much as a portrait was a handy picture of a duchess. To the Guild, a map was a binding contract with the ground. Drawn in guild ink from measurements that were both truthful and checked, a sheet could fix the land it described, so that a hill stayed where the chart said, a river kept its bed, and a road remained a road rather than wandering off in search of a more interesting county. The whole kingdom of Aster, from the sea-walls to the Marches, lay under such sheets, bound into the great Atlas like a quilt stitched over a restless sleeper. Where the sheets stopped, the land was loose, and loose land drifted.

Isla had grown up on the edge of that idea, in the river town of Corrin Ferry, where her father forged the great iron chains that held the ferries to their crossing. A chain, he told her, is not strong because of its links but because every link has been tested. She had carried that sentence all the way to Vell, along with a letter of introduction, a second-hand coat, and the dubious distinction of being the only scholarship apprentice the Guild had admitted in forty years. The other apprentices were the sons and daughters of magistrates and shipowners. They had tutors, and they had surnames that opened doors; hers, for reasons nobody had ever explained to her, seemed to close them.

"Corrin!" The voice came from the stairwell hatch behind her, light, fluting and delighted. "Are you taking the same angle a fourth time, or have you finally decided to marry it?"

Dorian Pike, third-year, climbed out onto the roof in a tailored navy coat with a gold watch chain looped across it like a tiny, expensive hammock. He had a face that always seemed on the verge of being photographed.
pages.image: On a slate guild roof at dawn, Dorian Pike, a smug nineteen-year-old with oiled brown hair, a tailored navy coat and a gold watch chain, climbs out of a stairwell hatch smirking, while in the foreground Isla in her mustard-yellow surveyor's coat, with ink-stained fingers and two brass pencils in her auburn hair knot, kneels beside her tripod-mounted brass sightglass and looks up at him with a flat, patient, unamused expression.

pages.text:
"Four readings," Isla said, without lifting her eye from the glass. "I haven't decided about the fifth."

"The Mint chimney has leaned since my grandfather was a boy. It is a landmark. People set their watches by it." Dorian leaned on the parapet and grinned at the city. "Let me spare you the next hour. It leans. Everything old leans. That is how you know it is old."

"If it leans," said Isla, "then something about the chimney is wrong. If it doesn't, something about the city is." She wrote the fifth angle down. "I would like to know which of us is mistaken."

"Us? Heavens. You do realize that this is a hobby for you, and a career for the rest of us?" He said it lightly, as though he were offering her a biscuit. That was the infuriating thing about Dorian: he never needed to be cruel, because he was so reliably, comfortably right about the way the world arranged itself. "Third-year placements are posted at nine. Half of us know where we are going, and the other half of us are Corrin."

Isla wrote the sixth reading in the margin, where it looked like a very small act of rebellion. Her hand did not tremble. It almost never did, and that, she suspected, was the only reason the Guild had kept her this long: a steady hand was a gift that could not be taught or bought, and even the most snobbish master could see the value of a line that came out true. She gathered her notebook, folded the tripod legs with a click, and said "Thank you for the weather, Dorian," and went down the stairs before he could think of an answer.
pages.image: Close on the roof, Dorian Pike in his navy coat with a gold watch chain leans on a stone parapet smiling lightly toward a city of chimneys, while Isla in her mustard surveyor's coat, two brass pencils in her hair, folds her brass tripod and heads for a stairwell door with calm dignity, a notebook under her arm.

pages.text:
The Atlas Room lay at the heart of the Guild, under a vault so high that its far corners dissolved into the dim like the corners of a cathedral. The sheets of the Atlas hung there on brass rails, each as tall as a door and as finely worked as lace, and at this hour, with the lamps unlit and the first sunlight pouring through the clerestory windows in long, slanting columns, they looked like the sails of some vast and motionless fleet. The hush was the sort that is made of paper. Isla slowed in it, as she always did, and, as always, felt her pulse settle against the quiet.

Master Orrin Vasht was asleep in a leather chair beneath the sheet of the Western Marches. He was sixty-three, with a close white beard, skin the deep brown of old walnut, a grey wool coat in which several decades of ink had settled like sediment, and a battered felt hat tipped over his eyes with a pencil tucked into the band. His walking stick lay across his knees. Isla had never learned whether he actually slept or merely found it the most convenient way to avoid listening to people he disagreed with.

"I am awake," said Master Vasht, without moving the hat. "I am merely allowing the day to arrive in its own time. What have you got?"

"A discrepancy," said Isla. "On the Mint chimney. It might be in the chimney. It might be in the city. It might be in me."

"Then it is almost certainly in you," said Vasht, tilting the hat up with one finger to reveal two shrewd grey eyes, "and we shall find out in a moment. Show me."

She laid her notebook open on his knee. He read it slowly, running a thick forefinger down the columns, and she watched his face, which gave nothing away. It never did. After a very long time he grunted and said "Six readings, from one tower, with one instrument." He did not say it unkindly. He said it the way a doctor says "temperature."
pages.image: Inside a vast hushed vaulted hall with tall pale map sheets hanging on brass rails like sails in slanting morning sunbeams, Master Vasht, a sixty-three-year-old man with dark-brown skin, a short white beard, a grey wool coat and a battered brown felt hat tipped up, sits in a leather chair with a carved walking stick across his knees reading Isla's notebook, while Isla in her mustard surveyor's coat stands anxiously beside him.

pages.text:
By half past eight they had read it again, with the second sightglass, from the opposite tower of the Guild, and Vasht had made Isla run the figures twice more on a slate while he sat with his hat over his eyes and listened to her chalk. At the end of it he asked her to say the answer aloud, which was one of his habits, and she found her voice came out smaller than she had hoped.

"The chimney is straight. It does not lean at all. Which means," she swallowed, "the Guild's own benchmark, the brass disc set in the floor of this very room, which the whole city of Vell is measured from, is off. By about the width of a hair."

"A hair," Vasht repeated. "That is a very small thing, Isla Corrin. And a very large one." He said it quietly, and for a moment he looked at the long shelf at the end of the Atlas Room, where one sheet hung blank among the finished ones: a plain, patient, unmarked oblong of the Guild's best paper, framed like a window onto nothing. It was the Unmade, the stretch of loose country at the kingdom's edge that nobody had ever charted. Isla had walked past it every day for two years and had never once seen him look at it directly.

A page boy burst through the double doors at a dead run, skidded on the polished floor, saved himself on a brass rail and gasped, "Master Vasht! The Queen sends. Noon, at the palace. For you and," he squinted at a paper, "your apprentice."

Isla glanced down at her ink-stained fingers and her very much slept-in coat, and then, helplessly, back at the blank sheet. She had the sudden, dizzying feeling of having walked into a room where her life had already been drawn, and it was waiting, very politely, for her to find out where the lines went.
pages.image: In the vaulted Atlas Room, Isla in her mustard surveyor's coat with two brass pencils in her auburn knot stands holding a notebook and staring up at one single large blank framed pale map sheet on the end of a row of finished detailed map sheets, her face wide-eyed and a little frightened; beside her old Master Vasht in his grey coat and felt hat leans on his walking stick watching her, and a breathless page boy in livery bursts through tall double doors at the back.
